utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, and Vladimir Santic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Biletic, could you please stand and make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, could I interrupt for one moment, Sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The Prosecution has one concern we would like to address Your Honours on very briefly, and that is regarding the witness Mr. Slavko Marin who was mentioned yesterday. This is not the normal run of witnesses, in terms that he was a designated alibi witness for the special defence. As a result, of course, there has been an investment of resources in a preliminary interview with that particular witness, and we were just wondering that taking account of the apparent significance of that person, we wonder whether the non-attendance is simply a logistical problem that may require him to be called later or something of that nature, or whether indeed it is the fact that the Defence either no longer intend to call him or, indeed, he has refused to testify or something of that nature. We feel perhaps in the circumstances it is appropriate that we should know precisely why this witness, at this stage, is suddenly dropped from the list. That's the only issue I would like to raise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic, could you clarify this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The real reason for the non-appearance of Slavko Marin at this moment, I don't know and I cannot tell you. We did all that is necessary to do when a witness is about to come. That was what we had agreed upon, and we expected the witness Marin to be here. I needed to tell you also that Defence complied with the request of the Chamber and enabled a meeting, an interview of the witness by the Prosecution, as to the alibi referred to. On the 10th of March, we had the interview with Mr. Slavko Marin and with Franjic at the time. Now, in June, on the 10th of June, also an interview was conducted with Mr. Biletic. We therefore complied with the decision of the Chamber to enable such an interview not less than a fortnight before their appearance before the Court. That is what I wished to add. However, as I have said, I really do not know the real reasons for the absence of Mr. Slavko Marin. I cannot confirm that Mr. Slavko Marin will not come or that he will come. I simply need time to see what was the reason. I shall do that this week. Mr. Slavko Marin is an important witness for us. I also have documentation showing my correspondence with the Ministry, the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He works there. I indicated in my letter and said that we expect this witness to turn up, that he's very important for the defence of Mr. Vladimir Santic. We want to see him here. I do not see why the Prosecution should be concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, firstly I can confirm very much the cooperation we received from my learned friend Mr. Pavkovic over these interviews. We did, indeed, in full measure, and for that we are grateful. I appreciate my learned friend's dilemma, so perhaps we can take it that Mr. Slavko Marin perhaps awaits in the wings and maybe will be accommodated at a later stage. I'm obliged to you. Thank you, Mr. Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Biletic, could you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. It is a common procedure for the witnesses to give their full name to the Court, so will you please do so, and also give us a few more usual particulars. Where were you born, when, your family status, your current address?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: My name is Davor Biletic. I was born in Zenica on the 1st of August, 1964. I am married, the father of two children. I don't know what else should I say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Biletic, I didn't hear, or perhaps I simply wasn't following. Did you tell us where you live now?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I live in Vitez on Petra Kresimira Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you only make a pause between the end of my question and the beginning of your answer because of the interpreters. Could you now tell us, where did you live before you came to live in Vitez sometimes in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I have spent all my life in Zenica, naturally, until 1992, and in Ive Andrica 9A Street in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you tell us that you spent your whole life in Zenica, could you tell us something about Zenica? All I really want to know is what is the ethnic structure of the Zenica population or, rather, what was it at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Ethnically speaking, the structure was -- I think the majority were Muslims, and the rest were Serbs and Croats. So about 50 per cent should be Muslims, and the other half should have been Muslims (sic) and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, could you tell us something about your education? What school did you come out of?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I came from the elementary school in Zenica, and then the secondary medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So what is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I'm a medical technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do? What was your job? Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: After I came out of this secondary school, I enrolled in high medical school straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time when you enrolled, you had first to serve the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: As soon as I finished my secondary school, I went into the JNA, and when I came back from the JNA, I couldn't find a job immediately in my profession, so I waited. That is, I was a waiter, that is, for some time, and after that I got a job with the Zenica Hospital, and I worked there until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What was your job or jobs in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I worked for the regional health centre. It was called Dzemal Bijedic at the time. I don't know what it is called today. I was at the surgical department, that is, intensive care unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Until when did you work in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I worked in Zenica, that is, until the October or November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What then? What kind of job did you have after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: After I left Zenica, I moved to Vitez because my closest friend, who at that time worked for the military police, he said that the military police were looking for a military policeman. The pay was very good, much higher than what I was getting at my former job, and that was why I accepted it, that is, I decided to get a job there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you moved to Vitez and got a job with the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: It was in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What is the name of your friend who mediated in your getting the job there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Mario Jurisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long -- so you arrived in November 1992 in Vitez, and how long were you in the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I was with the military police until 1997, when the reorganisation took place, or rather when the Federation army was established, and I still work for the army of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that before you applied for the job with the military police, you wanted to know what would be your duties and what were the tasks, what would be your tasks in the military police, so that you would know what you were getting into. Did you go to the military police as a military policeman, or as a medical technician?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, what should I call it? It's usually a dual role. You were both as a military policeman and a medical technician as the need arises. That is, I would extend first aid, for instance, if -- perish the thought -- something happened to someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But wasn't there somebody with a higher medical education than you in the military police, a physician or something?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't -- no, there wasn't, and we still don't have a physician. It is very difficult to find a physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, what was the responsibility of the military police at the time? I mean, its principal task.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: The task of the military police at that time was the protection of facilities, protection of people, control of roads, control of traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You are still with the army today, and I presume you are quite knowledgeable as far as the military organisation is concerned; could you tell us that today the military police still exercise the same function as at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I do not think that the responsibilities of the military police change. I think it is like that the world over. Protection of facilities, of people, of communications, protection of very important persons. For instance, protection of command posts, military transport, and things like that. I mean, these things do not change.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And when you got the job there, where was your workplace?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: When I came there, my workplace was at the explosives plant, the former Slobodan Princip Selo, that is SPS, and I worked there for a month, or rather about a month, because this was a plant of fundamental importance because it was part of the military industry, making explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: For about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: And after that I worked at the Vitez Hotel. Rather, I was with the security of the Vitez Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say "security of the hotel"; were you guarding the hotel as a facility, or somebody in that hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: We were guarding the hotel as a facility. Naturally, those who were in the hotel, by the same token, they were protected by us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say you were a medical technician and also a military policeman. Could you tell me, at that time, who was your immediate superior in the military police at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: My immediate -- my direct superior in the military police was Ivo Brnada.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, apart from the military police which had its headquarters there at the hotel, were there any other military personnel in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, there were military personnel. I used to see General Blaskic in the hotel, Slavko Marin, and some other people. Yes, sure, there were some other military people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So could one say that the military police, or rather you, provided security for them? For the general, you say: Was he a general at the time, General Blaskic? I think he was a colonel at the time; whom did he represent there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I don't think he was a colonel, even, then. I don't think there were any ranks at the time. I mean, people discharged duties; how should I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: In that hotel, the police also had their premises. Could you tell us which were the premises which the police were using?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: The police were using a room on the ground floor and some rooms on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How many soldiers, or rather how many members of the military police, were accommodated there? Were they all soldiers of the military police, or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: There were, as a rule, 10 to 15 military policemen resident there; that is, as far as I could judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And what was their duty, those who were accommodated in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, they were there to provide security for that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that the responsibility of the military police was to protect roads; could you tell us, which roads do you mean, do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military police provided security for roads; that is, Puticevo, Nova Bila, Vitez, Busovaca road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us go back to those military policemen who were accommodated in the hotel. You told us that it was their duty to guard the hotel and people in it. Those policemen in the hotel, did they sleep there also?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: They did -- well, it depended. If they were on duty, then they slept there. If not, then they went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But in view of the needs for security, could you tell us how many people -- that is, how many members of the military police -- were there in the hotel at any given time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: From 10 to 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sleep at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: At times I did, at times I went home. I mean, when I could, I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you try to recall the names of some persons who were members of the military police at the time and who were at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can remember a couple of people with whom I had struck a friendship. Mario Jurisic, Ivo Brnada, Nikica Safradin. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, when I say "at that time," I mean, of course, between November '92 until the 16th of April, 1993. So if I say "at that time," I mean that particular period of time. Those individuals you have just mentioned, did they discharge any special duties or tasks as military policemen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, they were just plain military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivo Brnada?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Ivo Brnada was our superior, our immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us -- I don't know if you know that -- in addition to the military police accommodated in the hotel, were there any other police in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: There was always, naturally, the civilian police, of course. They looked after the civilian structures of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say the civilian police who looked after the civilians, and so did the military police deal only with those matters that had to do something with the army?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, the military police dealt only with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So if a perpetrator of some wrongful act were a member of the military police, then it would be the duty of the military police to do something about it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So if an incident happened, if an event happened involving military people, then it would be the military police taking care of that particular incident; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, it would be the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And where was the seat of the military police? I mean, the hotel.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been some 80 metres below the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And at that time, could you tell us if the civilian police wore the same type of uniform as the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, they were still using -- I mean, those blue uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to several more questions about the hotel in which you were accommodated itself. The Hotel Vitez in Vitez, how many entrances did it have, or does it have?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it had several entrances, but one used only the front entrance, the main entrance into the hotel. But there were about three or four entrances, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that only one entrance -- that is, the main entrance -- was used; was it used by all those who came to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, one had to use this main entrance for security reasons. I mean, because at that time we were only an embryo of an army, and we were just learning everything from scratch, so that we were using only that one front entrance. We had read somewhere that for security purposes it would be better to have only one main entrance because it would make it easier to control the traffic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that other doors into the hotel were locked up? That one couldn't get in or come out through these other doors?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, they were locked, because security would lose any purpose if one could enter at a dozen different places. I mean, there would be no sense in having any security. So we used only one entrance, and all the other doors were locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that all the other doors were locked, is that an assumption on your part in order to show us that it stands to reason to control the movement of persons, or was it within your terms of reference that you went to check all these other doors and see whether they were locked?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, they were locked. It was the duty of the military policeman working at the reception desk to go and see whether the doors were locked. The doors were kept locked from the inside and outside. They had bolts and locks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you, who were involved in the security of the hotel, were you on duty around the clock? Were you on duty around the clock?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, those who were at the reception desk, they would have shifts of six hours; that is, work for six hours and then have a rest of six hours. Those guards who stood on duty outside, they would work for two hours and have a four-hour rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So there would be three persons on duty, if I understood you properly: One at the reception desk and two outside the hotel building itself; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes, there were always three persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So those who were outside the hotel would stand guard for two hours and the one at the reception desk for six hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise; I missed a question. Do you know who kept the keys to the other doors of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I think it was the director of the hotel. He kept the keys.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: He looked after them personally, or were they in the offices somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they were in the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You have just told us that there was a reception desk at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain to all of us what this looked like, what this place looked like where the person on duty at the reception desk worked?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: This was a desk and a chair right next to the main entrance to the Vitez Hotel, so the person on duty there would check the people going in and out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you, when you were at the reception desk, kept a record of people entering the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Of course, there was a book of people going in and out, and when someone came in to visit, we would write down when they had arrived, whom they had visited, when they had arrived and when they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you note down every person who came to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, we did not make records of the people employed in the hotel; the cooks, the civilians who are employed there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you write down the name of a colleague of yours, a military policeman who was not on duty, if he came?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. If we knew the person, we didn't see any reason to control their movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that at the entrance, there was this desk. Apart from this desk, was there any other spot on the ground floor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, there was an office where we spent our time when we were not on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a proper hotel reception there as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was behind our desk, some two or three metres behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that behind the reception, there was a room which was used by the military police as an official room?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. We might call it some kind of office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether this office was used by Mr. Vlado Santic, among others?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he used that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how many people -- I apologise. I have already asked this, so I withdraw this question. Can you tell me how many people would be on duty at one point?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: One person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your place?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: At the desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were the person working six-hour shifts?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I worked six-hour shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall the name of the person working as the hotel receptionist at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, because her name is the same as my wife's name. I only remember her first name. I think it was Gordana.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, I would now like to ask you to recall the 15th of April, 1993, and my question is: On the 15th of April, 1993, were you on duty at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of April, I was not on duty until midnight. On that day, I was supposed to go home. My best friend, Mario Jurisic, called me, but I had a meeting with my girl friend who is now my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, when did you take up your duty at the desk?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: At midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you rest up to that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sleep?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No. I went out. I had a date with my girl friend. Of course, there was a disco in the hotel and it was open, so we spent most of our time in the disco.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How can we be sure today that it is the 15th of April, 1993, you are now recalling?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, because that was the first time I experienced the horror of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Biletic, did you usually sleep at the hotel or did you commute to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I slept at the hotel, and sometimes I commuted to Zenica and went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So when you got a job at the military police, did you move to the hotel at once or did you commute from Zenica to Vitez for a time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I commuted, sometimes I spent the night at the hotel, depending on the situation, on how I felt, on my mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If we recall the 15th of April, 1993, you said that you were with your girl friend who is now your wife; you said that you spent the time up to midnight. Can you tell me whether on that day, there was anything unusual going on compared to the previous days?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I was not in the restaurant. As you said, I was in the disco. The day was no different from the days preceding it. The disco was quite full, as it was every evening. Everything was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you did not notice anything that would tell you that there was an unusual situation around the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice anything. It was a normal day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When I say "something unusual", I mean the arrival or departure of people, of soldiers.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No. It was a normal day, like every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you began your shift at midnight between the 15th and 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You were supposed to stay on duty until 6.00 a.m.; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after midnight? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I arrived at midnight. I read a book. I will never forget it. I even remember what the book was, the Aquatain Conspiracy by Ludlum. I was supposed to wake up the people who were supposed to stand guard outside the hotel in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So at 2.00 a.m., did you wake up the guards who were supposed to stand duty outside?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were supposed to wake up others at 4.00 to take up guard duty from 4.00 to 6.00?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall today the names of at least some of the persons you woke up that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only recall Berislav Margeta because I was on good terms with him. That's why I remember him. But since I had spent relatively little time there, I didn't know the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. I make mistakes too. So when did you wake him up, at 2.00 or at 4.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you were on your own at the desk after midnight?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was alone after midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody else come up to you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, no, only when the guards were changing shifts, then they would pass by.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether you recall what happened that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, that morning, around 5.00 or maybe a quarter past 5.00, Vladimir Santic came to work, as he did every morning. After that, around half past 5.00, 05.30 hours, there were powerful detonations. It could have been half past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you something else now. You said that at around a quarter past 5.00, Vlado Santic arrived as usual?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said "as usual", so this gives rise to a further question. Does it mean he always arrived that early?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was an early riser, and he always arrived early.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where was he employed?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I've already mentioned that there was an office behind the reception, and this is where he worked or, rather, where he spent the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Vladimir Santic come to work every day?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please wait.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he came every day, except on Saturdays and Sundays. But on working days, he came to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So that morning when he arrived, you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us again what time it was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: About a quarter past 5.00 or 20 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I know because there was a clock on my desk, because I had to know when I had to wake up the guards. I looked at the clock and I read the book, but I was always aware of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you had a clock or a watch on your desk so that you could wake up the soldiers on time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the guards who were supposed to stand guard outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning, did Vladimir Santic arrive on his own?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how he came? How did Vlado Santic come to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: He came on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that he came on foot?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I'm sure, because if he had come in some other way, I would have heard the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So if somebody had given him a lift in a vehicle, would you have registered this or would you have noticed it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I would have noticed it, because I had a good view from the desk because there were panes of glass, it was all glass. You could see outside, and also, of course, you could hear a vehicle arriving.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Vlado Santic lived at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. He lived in the building of the chess club. I don't know what the exact address is, but I know that the chess club was in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how far this is from the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps five or ten minutes on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go to visit Vlado Santic at his home?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. If there was a need, for example, if there was a traffic accident, we had to carry out an on-site inspection, we would go to get Vlado Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you saw where he lived?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So that is how you were able to estimate the time you needed to get to the hotel from his house?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, as you have told us today, you were employed in the police for about five years?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how the military police were trained in 1992 and 1993, up to April?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, the military police were --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What they wore. Sorry, not how they were trained; how they were dressed.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: They wore camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether the military police also had something to distinguish them from other soldiers? Some kind of patches?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, they wore white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: If we now recall that morning when Vlado Santic arrived, can you recall how Vlado was dressed that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: He was dressed the same way he was every morning, in a camouflage uniform. I know that he never liked wearing boots. He always wore shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, was he carrying a weapon?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. He always carried a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the other military policemen always carry a pistol?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, those of us who had a pistol, because the pistols there were issued, and most of us carried pistols. They were Russian pistols.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, then, whether Vlado was dressed the way military policemen were usually dressed that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was dressed the same as every morning, in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all military policemen carry pistols?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: As I said, some of them did not have pistols because there weren't enough to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the military police have other kinds of weapons at its disposal?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had automatic rifles, Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did every policeman have one Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was the same thing as with pistols. Not everyone could be issued with a rifle at that time, not everyone could be armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, when you were coming to take up your duties every day, have a Kalashnikov with you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Only the two guards standing guard outside had Kalashnikovs. The other rifles were locked up in a kind of locker behind the reception.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So only the policemen standing outside carried other weapons, long weapons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the other long weapons were locked up. Where was the room where the rifles were locked up?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: It was not a room, it was a locker. They were lined up and there was a chain going through them, and then there was a lock.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that these weapons were locked up. Who had access to the keys?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, we had to keep the weapons locked up because sometimes one or two rifles would go missing, and the keys were in the room where Vladimir Santic, Ivo Brnada, and others spent the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, at that time, did you know about a plan for emergency situations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a plan, if there was an attack, we would unlock the rifles. We would take the rifles, and all the guards would run to their places, because there is such a plan in every army in case of emergency situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So this plan envisaged that these rifles would be taken, and who would take them, and where they would go to stand guard?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's what the plan included.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning of the 16th of April, 1993, at about 5.00 or a quarter past 5.00, you saw Vlado Santic at the entrance and at your desk; did you have any conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, just the usual greetings: "Good morning, what's new," and so on. That was the usual kind of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: After this usual greeting, where did Vlado Santic go?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: He went to the room I have already mentioned, where he spent the time when he was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, how well or not do you know Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say I knew him well, but we would have a drink together sometimes, exchange a few words. So he's an acquaintance of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the situations you mentioned when you went to fetch him at his house, you did not carry on a private friendship with him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether at that time Vlado had any health problems?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know because we talked about it, because I was a medical technician, so sometimes he would complain to me. He had problems with his kidneys.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us recall that morning when Vlado arrived at a quarter past 5.00 or 20 past 5.00. What happened next? You said there were some explosions; can you describe what happened?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, at about half past 5.00, maybe a minute or two later, first there was an extremely powerful detonation. After this, I left my book and went to the entrance of the hotel to see what was going on. After that, there were several more detonations, which made the glass, the windowpanes shake, and some of them shattered. After that I withdrew from the windows and stood behind a pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you determine the direction from which these projectiles came?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I could not at the time, because I didn't really know much about the army and the military. Being a medical technician, I knew more about medicine than the army. But now that I have been in to the army for such a long time, and all the additional training that I had, now perhaps I could make a relatively educated guess. One can never determine with certainty where an explosion comes from, or rather where a particular projectile has been fired from. Unless you see it, you can never establish it with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But apart from this artillery fire -- that is, shells and so on and so forth -- was there any infantry gunfire?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, in addition to cannon fire and these shells, there was also fire from rifles. There were bullets whizzing all around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And the hotel, was it particularly subjected to fire from all these weapons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, most of these shells and bullets were falling around the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When this thing that you are describing happened, where were other military policemen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, some five or six minutes after it all started, they all ran down from the rooms in which they were staying and ran down to the hotel lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Were the guards deployed outside the hotel, those who were on the outside security?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In all this melee that ensued, in all this fracas that ensued, some people ran out, snatched those rifles, and ran to posts they were supposed to take in case of an attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: After the alert, I went down to the main entrance and took my position some three metres from this entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And at the moment when the panic that you have just described began, and you took a position in front of the hotel, in front of the main entrance, can you remember if you perhaps saw Vlado Santic amongst those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see Vlado Santic. But as I was coming out, I only heard his voice. I mean, there was confusion all around, and I was -- also, of course, I was pretty frightened, like everybody else; I panicked. I remember his voice. I remember some details, for instance, saying, "What's this?" I just heard a voice behind me, but I was already at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm with certainty today that it was Vlado Santic's voice that you heard?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it was Vlado Santic's voice that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were two or three metres away from the front entrance, and you came out, and then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Because I was in the open, in view of these explosions, and behind me were all those huge glass panes, I just froze, as we put it in our military slang, behind this small wall, and hoped that nothing would hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: From the place where you took your position, did you have an unimpeded view of the entrance into the hotel, towards the receptionist's?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that place is about three, maybe four metres from the entrance into the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And was it possible for someone to go into the hotel and come out of it without you noticing him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if you saw somebody else whom you knew apart from Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: You mean through the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I did. I can remember Ivica Franjic. He also worked there, and he would come to work every morning. He was the hotel manager, I believe. And two other blokes, I believe, working for the communication centre, or rather at the post office, which is not far from the hotel. I think the first name of one of them is Kruno, and the other one's I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us a while ago that you had a good view of the entrance and that you could see who was going in or coming out of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see the manager of the hotel come out of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, just a few moments after he had got in, I think not more than a couple of minutes later, he again left the hotel -- I mean, left -- I mean, he just ran out of the hotel, rather than left the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, how long did you remain at that place which you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, that is -- with some interruptions, I was there the whole day. I was there until about 11.00, when I felt rather peckish, so that I went into the hotel to get a sandwich.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did take it take to you get the sandwich from the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, not more than five minutes or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone go in or out of the hotel at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: The movement around the hotel was at the minimum. It was really very dangerous to move around there, to go in or out, so that nobody moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And where is that place where you took that sandwich in relation to your place?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been some five or ten metres, perhaps, from the front entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you see the entrance from that place?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No. No, but I just went in, took the sandwich, and went out. It could have been perhaps five minutes altogether that I was away from my post.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone take your place there at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, nobody else would take my place there, but there was usually somebody in the passage, in the hallway. But no, there was nobody replacing me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was around 11.00?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And the explosions in the town and around the hotel were just as intensive as in the morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, the intensity of explosions and gunfire had abated by that time, but it was still very dangerous. But it was lesser then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you see Vlado Santic again, I mean, that morning?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I saw him there as I was getting my sandwich, I saw Vlado Santic there. He had also presumably come to have a bite or something, but at any rate, I saw him there. When I took my sandwich, I was coming out, and then I saw Vlado Santic there. It could have been around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what Vlado was doing at the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: He just passed by me and went into this -- what should I call it -- this restaurant, this mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if he was wearing the same clothes as in the early hours of the morning, as you told us?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was wearing the same clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So wearing the same clothes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me, at that time, sometime around lunchtime, did any vehicle come to the hotel? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, a vehicle of the former UNPROFOR -- that is, the then-UNPROFOR, now SFOR -- an APC arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why they came there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: They brought two HVO members. I remember the names. One was Prskalo, and the other one, Zoran Pilicic or Milicic; I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, why did they come?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I did not know at the time. I mean, I don't know why they came and why they came by an UNPROFOR vehicle, why it was they who brought them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what happened to them in front of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: As soon as they got off the APC, they said goodbye to UNPROFOR members, and there was fire from infantry weapons, and the two of them were hit. And I do apologise, but they were hit in their behinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the hotel entrance that we talked about was very dangerous for all those bent on entering it or coming out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it was very dangerous. Even I, when I just peeped out, I guess it was a fragmentation bullet which fell just in front of me, and I was hit in the shin. But the fragments of these bullets are very small, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you saw Vlado Santic at lunchtime, sometime around 11.00 or after 11.00. Did you see Vlado Santic again that day?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did see Vlado Santic sometime around 18.00 in the evening, when I left the place where I was and went to have my dinner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, where was it that you saw Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, in that restaurant room, in the mess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: During dinner?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in the hotel that night?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Until about 20.00; that is, until it grew dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us if Vlado Santic was also in the hotel until that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: In all likelihood, yes, because the movements about were still at the minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And were you there after 20.00?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: After 20.00, six or seven of us were taken by a vehicle to the Bungalow, the so-called Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Before you left, did they tell you where you were going?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, Ivo Brnada, the one we already mentioned, he just remarked that we were going to the Bungalow. And we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you why you were going?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think -- I think confusion still reigned, and I don't think anybody knew, really, or said anything. Somebody said to get ready, a van would be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And was it also said that all of the members of the security from the hotel would go?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we all had to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you if all had to go.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: We were told that we would all be going.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And it was also said that you would be going to the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What did you know about the Bungalow before that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew that it was a restaurant or a hotel of sorts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you go to the Bungalow before that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How did you get to the Bungalow, those six or seven of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: We boarded then with the driver, and I remember the driver, Nikica Safradin. So he was -- that is who took us by that vehicle to the Bungalow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how others got to the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, which road did you take?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, because the lights on the vehicle were off, because the fire was still going on from infantry weapons, mostly, and a shell here and there, we were moving very slowly, by unknown -- taking an unknown route. Yes, we did make a round through the town, but it was very dangerous to move around. The risk was very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that around 8.00 or, rather, around 20.00 was when you set off. Do you remember, how long did this ride last?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it lasted some 35, perhaps 40 minutes, perhaps slightly longer. I cannot remember exactly, but it took a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that there was six or seven of you in that vehicle; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now try to remember the names of some of your fellow policemen?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, there was this one, as I have already mentioned, Margeta, [indiscernible], Nikica Safradin. I didn't know those others well enough, and a long time has passed by. I cannot remember the names. I do remember some faces, but not so the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if Vlado Santic was one of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, he was not with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the Bungalow, did you see Vlado Santic then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: When we got to the Bungalow, after a while, perhaps some 20 minutes later, I saw Vlado Santic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in front of the Bungalow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Oh, well, some 20 minutes, plus or minus, and we straightaway headed for some positions. We were taken there by some people, but it was dark and I couldn't see my way around. Only after a certain time, I learned that I was at a defence line called Kratina, so at a kind of a defence line; Kratina, Kuber, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us when you came to the military police or, rather, when you moved to Vitez, so you were not really familiar with the area, were you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't familiar with it, because I came from Zenica, so I knew the area very little.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay on those positions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that at the time, we were there for about ten days, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is, until the 26th of April, '93?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, after those 10 or 11 days, I came back to the hotel, to the Vitez Hotel, to work again with the security there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you went back to your former duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Vlado Santic afterwards?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him when I came back to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I saw him in the hotel lobby.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should like to conclude my examination now. That is, I do have three photographs which I should like to show to the witness to simply mark some of the locations that he referred to. I think it might take more than five minutes, which is as much as we have until the break, and so do you think we should go into the break now or should we continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No, we should continue, because actually today, since we have to stop at 1.00, we'll take our break at quarter to 11.00. There's only one break, and so we can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, will the usher please take over these photographs for the Chamber and the Prosecution and to place one of these photographs on the ELMO so that the witness could comment on its contents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first photograph will be marked D10/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, will you please take a look at this photograph? This photograph was taken on the 10th of June this year, and this is the entrance into Hotel Vitez. Have there been any changes between the 16th of April, 1993, and today? Is there any change in the appearance of the hotel, as you see it in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, there has been no change.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that there was only one main entrance into the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the one where we have "Hotel Vitez" written, but we see on this photograph yet another entrance, but it was locked and I do not think it is in use today even.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please then mark with "1" the main entrance into the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And put "2" to mark the side entrance.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Biletic, you told us that you had come out and were in front of the hotel. Could you roughly show where the position was? I'm afraid I was a very poor photographer. I didn't take really a good view, but could you please try to show us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphone of the witness be switched on, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you put an "X" next to the place and the number "3"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it should be somewhere where this vehicle is (indicating), perhaps a metre, a metre and a half, the very edge of the building, the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So at this place where you put that "3", that is the place where that morning, on the 16th of April, 1993, you spent the whole day, practically?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the whole day, practically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Biletic, I should like to show you another photograph taken at the same time and, Mr. Usher, will you please take care of them. Give them to the Chamber and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The second photograph will be marked D11/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, is that the receptionist's area and the desk?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the receptionist's here behind these flowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I already told you that this photograph was taken this year, but is it the same as it was on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So will you now please put a cross next to the place where your desk was, and then put a "1" next to it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, the desk was about here (indicating), except that it was placed lengthways as against -- that is, perpendicular to the receptionist's.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So behind that desk, we see the receptionist's desk here. Could you put "2" next to the receptionist's desk?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, is that the area where you heard Vlado Santic's voice as you were coming out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the area where you saw Vlado Santic the first time when he came for work?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now I should like to show you yet another photograph, and I shall ask you to comment on it, only in demonstration of some of the things you said today. Usher, will you please take care of these? For the record, I would like to -- I apologise. For the record, I would like to repeat that this photograph 2 was taken on the 10th of June this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are there any changes compared to the time that we are talking about today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I can't see any changes. Everything is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So this is the receptionist's area we just talked about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Behind the reception, and this is where the coat of arms is, we see a door. Is that the entrance to the rooms you talked about which were used by the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, behind this door is the room where the military police spent their time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that door with the number "1"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: (Witness marks)

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: That is all. Thank you, Mr. Biletic. I have no further questions for you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The third photograph will be marked D12/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I forgot to tender these three photographs into evidence as Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution, so they are admitted into evidence. I assume there's no cross-examination by other Defence counsel, so we can move to the Prosecution. I don't see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. Biletic, good morning to you. My name is Michael Blaxill, and I am one of the prosecuting counsel in this case. In view of what you've said here today, I do have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell me how many entrances or exits there were on the ground floor of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: On the ground floor, there were four, four entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: On floors above that, were there any fire escape type of exits?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, there was a fire escape which I have already mentioned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you've said that the keys for all the doors of the building that were locked were kept in the hotel director's office; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: When you did desk duty like you did on the night of the 15th to the 16th of April, did you have any personal duty to check the doors or to check the keys, or was that not part of your duties?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was usually checked by Ivo Brnada, who was our commander, and on several occasions I checked it myself. And the guards standing outside would report if anything was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I can move to the specific night of the 15th to the 16th of April, 1993, did you in fact perform any check that night or was that done by other people?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I personally did not check those doors that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you were in a battalion of the military police. That was the military police of the HVO, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I believe your unit was known as the 4th Battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Within that battalion, is it correct they had a number of companies, one of which was based at the Hotel Vitez, or the command of it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't know, I couldn't say, because I was just an ordinary soldier or military policeman, and I did not know what the organisation was or how many companies there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So let's take it from your position. Did you form part of a kind of platoon of people, and if so, how many people were in that platoon or group that you belonged to? If you recall, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we might call it a security platoon for the security of facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: All right. The commander of that platoon was Mr. Brnada; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew only Mr. Brnada as my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But you said that the military police that you belonged to overall also had duties for road security and looking after traffic matters and things like that, so presumably there were other platoons, were there, of people to do those duties?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It is what I said means that there was a platoon taking care of traffic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is it also a fact that within the overall structure, there was what they called an anti-terrorist platoon, a special type of unit? Did you recall anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly whether there was an anti-terrorist platoon, because it was just being established. We were only beginning to establish our army. We were just learning. It would be different now, after we have gone through military training. We know how an army has to be set up. But at that time, there was a lot of confusion, so I can't say whether there was an anti-terrorist platoon. But as far as the traffic platoon is concerned, they were ordinary military policemen. They were not specialists. They weren't specially trained even for traffic, let alone terrorism, combating terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Does the name "Jokers" mean anything to you in the context of military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Not in the context of the military police, but I have heard about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: What was your impression of what the Jokers were? Can you say what sort of unit they were?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. I can't say, as a military policeman or a medical technician. I cannot know at that time who or what the Jokers were.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let's move to the location of the Bungalow which you eventually went to on the night of the 16th. Did you know at that time what the Bungalow was, in terms of any military people who were based there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: All I knew, that the Bungalow was some kind of catering facility on the road. I didn't know that there were any soldiers stationed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, on the evening of the 15th of April, you say you reported for duty on the desk at midnight; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was everything quiet in the hotel at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Perhaps a few people were watching television at that time, but it was very quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall anybody entering the hotel or leaving the hotel, say, between midnight and the time you woke the next guard shift at 2.00?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: The guard -- the shifts outside were changed, and I think that from midnight until 2.00 a.m., no one came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How many people were physically on guard on each shift? How many men were on duty?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Between -- there were always between 10 to 15 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Physically on duty at one time? I mean how many were there per shift of guys who would actually be out guarding?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Three men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: The others would be resting, waiting their turn; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, as far as you were aware, in the early hours of the 16th of April, this was, I guess, just a night's duty like any other; would that be fair to say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was just an ordinary night.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So basically you spent some, I would imagine, some rather boring hours just sitting at the desk, but you would occupy your time by reading your book?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't boring, because it was a very good book. He was a very good writer, so I wasn't bored in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And it seems that nothing happened during the night that caused you any sudden concern or made that night any different to any other night; you simply had to make sure you woke up the guards at the right times?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill, should we perhaps take our recess now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I think it is an opportune moment, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Blaxill?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, on the night in question, the 15th to 16th of April, 1993, was General Blaskic -- or then, I believe, Colonel Blaskic -- in residence at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think he was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was Mr. Slavko Marin also in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he slept in the hotel, but I think I saw Slavko Marin in the morning, which means that he probably was in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From where you were doing your duty at the desk, would you know whether those gentlemen would be working in the night? I mean, if they were working in their command centre, would you have knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't be able to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And just to check another aspect, possibly, of your duties, or not, if any military orders were issued by those people at any time, would they in any way involve you on the desk, to pass them on to someone, or to have them pass by you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No. My duty was security. I was only interested in who was going in and out. I had no control over other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: From the performance of those duties, do you recall whether Mr. Blaskic and his officers used couriers to come in and collect stuff and take stuff away?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what they used or who they used. Perhaps there was a method, but as an ordinary military policeman, I was not interested in that, and I wasn't able to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So at the present time, sir, we basically have a situation that this was a very unremarkable night. It was quiet, it was boring, but you at least had the stimulus of a good book to read. Would that sum up the evening?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably a good description of that night. If I had supposed that any kind of conflict or something was going to happen, I would probably have got my parents and my brother out of Zenica. They spent the whole war there. If I had known something was going to happen, I would have brought my parents to Vitez so they could be with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So we now move to the early part of the morning when people start to arrive for work. Was Mr. Vlado Santic the first person to turn up, to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the first to come to work. He usually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, in the scheme of things, you said your immediate superior was Mr. Brnada; but to your knowledge, was Mr. Santic senior to Brnada in the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the chain of command was at that time, and I can't say whether he was senior to Mr. Brnada.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You say you were serving in a platoon that was based at the Hotel Vitez, sir, and you didn't know who was the most senior military policeman in the building?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested. I knew of only one superior to me, and he was the one I was to turn to and the one who gave me orders if there was anything I had to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: But in your dealings with Mr. Santic, you surely must have found out something as to what he did. I believe you said you had had a coffee or a drink with him from time to time. Did you not know roughly what his position was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that he was an investigator, that he carried out on-site inspections when there was a traffic accident, which means he wasn't an ordinary policeman, he knew more than others did, because you had to have special training to do that kind of investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Brnada ever say to you who his boss was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: We never went into that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, sir, was it dark or was it light at the time Mr. Santic arrived at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was semi-light, semi-dark. It was neither light nor dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And Mr. Santic arrived, and he arrived in every way as he normally did. He was dressed the same, he greeted you in the same way. It was, again, unremarkable that he should turn up then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. It was a normal day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
