utterances.text: So in fact, Mr. Biletic, there would have been nothing particular that would make you notice the time that specific day; in fact, is it not that you just had the impression that things were as normal? To the best of your recollection, that was the time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have already said, if I had known that anything was happening or was about to happen, of course I would have taken care of my parents. I would have let them know that they should get out of Zenica. I wouldn't have left them there for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that you assumed that it was the usual time that Mr. Santic arrived, rather than specifically checking on the clock? That's what I'm trying to suggest, sir.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, since I was sitting at the desk -- it was like this (indicating), but it was a bit longer -- so it was my custom to look at the clock all the time because it was -- the time was drawing near when I was supposed to wake up the next guard shift, so I kept glancing at the clock. And when he was passing by and I looked up, I glanced at the clock because I was thinking about having to wake up the next guard shift.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So Mr. Santic has now arrived for work; how long was it, do you think, between that arrival and the start of the detonations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps about 15 or 20 minutes. I can't be precise to the minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And the moment you heard those first detonations, what did you do, exactly? What was the very first thing you did?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you, I stated that I was going to tell the truth, so I'm going to tell you that I was more frightened than ever in my life. When the detonations began, I looked for shelter because there was a lot of glass near my desk, and I was afraid of being hurt by the glass or something else that might come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And so this shelter, was this within the building, initially, inside the building?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Inside the building, nearby, there was a pillar. It was near the staircase.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you took cover from the -- obviously from the risk of flying glass -- behind the pillar. And then what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: After that, chaos set in. People came out of their rooms, there was confusion, chaos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was there much shouting and voices competing with each other as people spoke?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes, there was a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And of course we have the additional fact that there are shells falling and there are bullets flying around the building, to add to the confusion and the noise. Did you receive any kind of instructions then as to what to do?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Of course. Someone unlocked the rifles, so we took our rifles, and every guard went to his post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you remember who unlocked the rifle rack?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Truth to tell, I have no idea. I just can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall if any one of your colleagues spoke to you, sort of said, "Hey, grab a rifle," or something? Did anybody speak to you directly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Everything was happening very quickly, very fast. I mean, when it calmed down a little bit, after we pulled ourselves together, after some 10 or 15 minutes, then yes, we knew the procedure, we knew what we had to do, and then awaited what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall who actually handed you a rifle? Or did you take it yourself from the rack?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I did it. I did it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you then, I believe, went outside the front of the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long do you think it was between your hearing the first detonation and your leaving the building to take a post outside?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been an hour; perhaps less, perhaps more. I'm not really sure. 40, 50 minutes, an hour. I'm not sure about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you are saying from the first detonations you were actually in the building for an hour, nearly an hour, before you went outside? I believe you said during that hour, if that's the time period, you didn't actually see Mr. Vladimir Santic -- is that right? -- yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not, no. After he came to work, I did not see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Well, having given us the description you have, of a babble of voices, you can't remember who spoke to you directly, there's chaos, there's noise, there's guns going off, are you sure now that you can say that you recognised the voice of Vlado Santic saying, "What is this?" That's a remarkable thing to remember, sir, with respect, in all that chaos, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Some details stuck in my mind as if in a slow motion film. For instance, windowpanes bursting, and Vlado Santic's voice. I'm positive that it was his voice. I mean, one remembers some details, and others one doesn't. But I remember it as I was going out. It was some two or three metres behind me, and I just heard his voice distinctly. These are moments when one simply does not remember anything, but it registers somehow. It just sticks in one's mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Where were you when you noticed the arrival of Mr. Franjic, the hotel manager?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I was behind that pillar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And you say that a few minutes later, you ran out of the building again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, quite. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And was this by the front door, you say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: And is that just -- I mean, again, is there any special reason why you should remember that fact, when you consider the overall chaos of things going on around you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I know, that is, that immediately after that manager, Ivica Franjic, two other blokes came in. I remembered one of them, and we were rather close; his name was Kruno. And that is why I remembered it, because Franjic also came in every morning. He had to take care of the menu, or whatever he had to do as hotel manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then say he ran from the building, but wasn't it true that at that time the front door was, I believe you said, a very dangerous place to use? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: So it was, very dangerous. But I ran out, and so did Franjic. He was moving very fast. You know, there were such intervals of time when, for some five or ten minutes, a ghost-like silence would reign, and there would be this lull, which was like a ghost-like lull, and we would use that to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Is there any possibility you might be mistaken on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you took up station outside the Hotel Vitez, and you found protection behind a wall; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You stayed there at least until something around 11.00 in the morning, did you then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Was the building still under heavy fire either by artillery or small arms at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: There was still infantry fire and some artillery, but intensity had significantly abated as against what was happening in the early morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you're saying the conditions had eased sufficiently that it was safe enough to go and find something to eat rather than remain behind the wall?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't really know. It didn't really matter whether I thought the situation had significantly calmed down or not. I was simply famished, and I decided I had to go and get something to eat or I might have fainted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you went back inside the Hotel Vitez and found something to eat at the canteen area, is that right, or restaurant?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You saw Mr. Santic there at that time, 11.00?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say exactly to the minute, but it could have been at 11.00, 11.15 that I saw Mr. Santic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Were there any other people at that time in there taking a break of some description?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that, because I simply got the sandwich and went back to the place where I had been from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, when you deployed to that position outside Hotel Vitez, had you received an order from anybody to do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: That was a post assigned to me by that plan, by that plan of alert, of alarm. If anything happened, then I would have to go to that particular post.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So this was a kind of standing order for an emergency, and you just simply followed that order; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you might say that, in case of an emergency, an alarm or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you then returned to your position outside the building. Do you remember if any people were coming and going, say, around midday time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Around midday? I wouldn't say so, no. The movements were reduced to a minimum, because at that time people still didn't know what was going on. Nobody could give any exact information as to what was going on or what was the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So is it correct that then essentially for the rest of the day, you just remained on guard until, I think, about 18.00 hours? You remained on guard at that location outside the building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I remained at that same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, you have made reference to the arrival of an UNPROFOR vehicle and its passengers getting out to enter the hotel and being wounded. Now, what time of day do you say that vehicle came to Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: It was in the morning. It could have been around 10.00, but I'm not sure. I remember that scene. I do not know the time, but I remember that scene when they were wounded, those two. That is, these were only slight injuries. Thank God nothing serious happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now, in another trial in this Tribunal, that of General Blaskic, there has been evidence given by, in fact, Mr. Marin relating to that incident, and that was to the effect that Mr. Zoran Pilicic, for one, had been to a meeting between the parties, the Bosnian army people and the HVO, and that returning to the Hotel Vitez and getting out of an UNPROFOR vehicle, he had been shot and wounded, as you have described. The only thing is both that witness, Mr. Marin, and indeed General Blaskic himself say that happened on the 17th of April, which would be a day later. Have you any observation you can give me on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Mr. Prskalo who was wounded, and Zoran Prskalo perhaps, but the entrance was under fire all the time. I can't really say, but I do think it was on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Now thinking again about it, sir, are you saying you can't be absolutely sure?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I believe it happened on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You then encountered Mr. Santic again at about 18.00 hours that afternoon, the 16th of April; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, around 6.00, around 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: How long were you in his presence at that time? I mean did you just pass each other by, or were you in his presence for a few minutes, or what was the nature of that encounter?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it could have been three or four minutes or even less perhaps, because we had all got there to have a meal in the restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So if I can encapsulate, and I hope that I do so correctly, Mr. Biletic, you see Mr. Santic for a few seconds at around 5.00, you see him again very briefly around 11.00, and you see him again briefly around 18.00 hours in the afternoon; is that a fair assessment by me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Why, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then after your dinner, you had a couple of hours until 8.00. What were you doing during that period? Were you back on guard or were you stood down to have some rest?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go back to guard there. I sat there in the restaurant for a while, and I even fell asleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So I would imagine then, sir, the fighting or the shelling and the shooting must have died down considerably by that time for you to be able to relax enough and sleep.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Honestly speaking, I do not think so, but I was simply so exhausted that I simply dropped off. I did close my eyes. But yes, yes, it was less intensive, both the cannon fire and the infantry fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Then around 20.00 hours, Mr. Brnada instructs six or seven of you to go across to the Bungalow, and you left Hotel Vitez by vehicle. What were the conditions at that time, sir? What were the conditions in terms of any shooting or shelling? Was it still dangerous?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. The fire was still going on. One could hear the shooting, but it was of a much lesser intensity than in the beginning. The situation, nobody knew what the situation was, and if you don't know what is happening and what is the situation, then of course it is dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: You were driven down from Vitez. Was that on the main road, to your recollection? I'm not absolutely certain if you said that. From the main road towards Nadioci where the Bungalow was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, I am from Zenica, and we travelled with our lights -- with car lights off. I could not really say where we were passing because it was already -- the night had already fallen and I'm not really familiar with the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Let us say, then, from what little you may have seen from the inside of the vehicle, did you appear to be on a properly made road or was it on some little dirt track? I mean could you tell the difference to that extent?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, we would spend some time on the asphalt, perhaps a few minutes on the asphalt, but I think -- I know that we made a circle around the town to avoid those areas exposed between the buildings, but I'm really not certain. I really don't know which route we took and whether it was macadam or asphalt. By that time, I was really quite confused and quite exhausted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you then arrived at the Bungalow. Were there many soldiers present at the Bungalow at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I cannot say how many of them, but roughly there was a group of soldiers. How many exactly, I could not say, because it was dark already and we did not go into the Bungalow when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: So you stopped outside the Bungalow. So in fact were these soldiers, however many, were they also outside the Bungalow itself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, several, yes, there were several of them in front of the Bungalow, moving about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: In relation to the building of the Bungalow itself, where was Mr. Vlado Santic when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I did not quite understand the question. Sorry, what do you mean "in relation to the building"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'll make myself clearer. When you arrived at the Bungalow, you said you saw Mr. Vlado Santic. Where was he? Was he outside the building, was he standing in the road; can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: He was in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Do you recall if he said anything when you and your colleagues pulled up outside?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't think he said anything, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you get out of the vehicle at all?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Can you recall from whom the instructions came for you to go up to the lines?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, it was Ivo Brnada who said it. He must have talked to someone, and that one had told him that we would be going to the line, so we were assigned a guide and went to the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, see Mr. Brnada talk to anyone?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, not really, I did not see Mr. Brnada talk to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, sir, after that you served ten days at the lines in Kratine, returning to Vitez on the 26th of April. Is that correct, is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I learned afterwards that that line was called Kratine or Kuber, and after some 10 or 11 days, I came back to Vitez. It could have been 10 or 11 days. I'm not quite sure how long I spent there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: May I have your indulgence for a moment, please, Your Honours. That concludes my questioning. Thank you very much, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Biletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, on the 16th of April, 1993, when you saw Vlado in the morning, and then until 22.00 or, rather, 20.00, before you went to the Bungalow, could Vlado Santic have left the hotel without your seeing him from the post which you held?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Nobody could go through the main entrance without my seeing him. That is why I was posted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that other entrances were locked. Does that mean that people could not use any other entrances?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I suppose one could not go out through other entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I do not understand. Why do you say "I suppose"? Are you sure about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, since those entrances were locked both from the inside and from the outside, I mean that one could not use those entrances.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Biletic, have you heard about special-purpose units?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have heard about their existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Were those special-purpose units part of your unit?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I had no way of knowing that, nor can I say anything about it. Of course, I knew people who worked with me because I was there for a very short -- I had worked for the military police for a very short time, and I simply had no way of knowing anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: To make it quite clear, you said that you were a member of a unit, the task of which was to provide security; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. My unit was guarding facilities, people, roads, like any other military police in the world, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So within that unit, and I'm not going into its strength or whether it was a platoon, a company, whatever, but within that unit of yours, were there any individuals who could be said to have belonged to a special-purpose unit, or were they only assigned to security, for security purposes?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: My unit was responsible only for security, as I have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But did Jokers -- was that the name of the special-purpose unit, Jokers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. At that time, I had no way of knowing that Jokers existed or who they belonged to. I really cannot say who was their commander. I really don't know and didn't know about those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you. I understand that you were just a plain, ordinary policeman and that you had nothing to do with military issues, but what I'm asking you has nothing to do with the knowledge about some very important military matters. My question is very simple. At that time, you did not know about Jokers?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I said I had heard about Jokers, but I did not know what they were. I already said at the very beginning that I had heard about Jokers, but I did not know what their duties were or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that Vlado Santic was clever, and you did not see him as an ordinary policeman; is that so?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I do not think he was an ordinary military policeman, because one must know certain things. I was not an ordinary soldier, a policeman, because I know how to give an injection or infusion or something like that. An ordinary policeman, military policeman, could hardly know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So perhaps he knew certain things and had some duties, but at that time you did not know exactly what was his rank?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and others treated him with deference, with respect. I didn't know what he was, but I know he went out to do on-site investigations in case of traffic accidents or perhaps an offence committed by a military policeman or a military person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that at that time, it was all in a very early stage, an embryonic stage, and that there were no ranks at the time such as are common in an army and on the basis of which one can conclude who is who?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally there were no ranks at the time. The ranks, that is, began -- that is, I was accorded a rank in '95. I doubt if anyone had any rank prior to '95. Naturally, in the army of the Federation, that was already the second period of its formation. That is, in the army of the Federation, that is, the army of B and H, now we have ranks, as in all the armies in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: From your desk, when you started towards the exit, and a few metres away you stopped and remained at that same place until 11.00, at least, and you said that behind you, a few steps behind you, you heard the voice, and you're telling us that that voice belonged to Vlado Santic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that it was as near, that it was as close, and that you had no doubt in your mind and that you can affirm it today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, right behind me. I cannot say whether it was a metre or two or three, but I clearly heard Vlado Santic's voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could one say that today you are not quite certain whether the person who was hit, the person who came by an UNPROFOR van, was a person named Prskalo or a person named Pilicic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: I think that person was called Prskalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the 16th of April, 1993, did you have any wartime experience, any combat experience?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, all I had was that in 1984, I did my regular service for the Yugoslav People's Army, for the JNA. But after that I had no experience with the military at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You described to us the time and the situations in which on the 16th of April, 1993, you saw and heard Vlado Santic. And it transpires from that that until 8.00 in the evening that day, you were having intermittent contact with Vlado Santic; is that true?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you told us also that after that, you went to the Bungalow, and that some of you, several of you, went by a van?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did all of those who were with the security team go to the Bungalow that evening? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, we were told in the evening that we would all be leaving the hotel and going somewhere. At that time, we did not know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that when you got to the Bungalow, you saw Vlado Santic standing in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, when had Vlado Santic got there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR BILETIC
utterances.text: No, I had no way of knowing that at that time. I simply could not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have no questions for the witness. Mr. Biletic, thank you for giving evidence in court. You may now be released. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Franjic. Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Counsel Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Witness. I would like to ask you to introduce yourself to the Court.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Good day. My name is Ivica Franjic. I was born on the 28th of February, 1956, in the village of Kruscica in the Vitez municipality. I am married, I have four children and a wife, and I now live in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak up a little and a bit closer to the microphone. You say, "I am now living in the Vitez municipality"?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us your address?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I live in Kralja Kresmira Cetvrtog Street, in an apartment in my family house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So what is your job today?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I'm a private entrepreneur.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you lived and worked before the war?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I lived in my family house in Kruscica in the Vitez municipality. I was employed in the Kruscica-Vitez catering company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What did that catering company consist of, the Kruscica-Vitez company? I would like to clarify my question: What work units were there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, there were two hotels. One of them was in Vitez, in the town, and it was called the Hotel Vitez. The other was in the village of Kruscica; it was called the Kruscica Hotel. And there were other catering establishments, such as restaurants, cafes. There were also some shops.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me until when you were employed in this company and what your position was?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: My last working day was the 15th of April, 1993, if we can say that. That was the last day I worked normally, and then I continued in that company for a while, performing duties -- actually, when the conflict broke out, I was the director of the Kruscica-Vitez catering company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we say that you were the director of the Vitez Hotel at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was the manager of Vitez Hotel, and the acting director of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were responsible for the situation in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, for the personnel employed in the hotel, I was the person in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you say that you worked until the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that on that day, you were in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about a hotel; is that the Vitez Hotel in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: To make it quite clear that we are talking about a certain hotel. I would now like to ask a question which I have asked before, but I would like to know if you recall the 15th, your last day at work. Can you tell us whether this was an ordinary day like all other days, or did you notice any events that caused you to pay special attention?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: It was a normal working day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when you left the Vitez Hotel on that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I think it was around 4.00 or half past 4.00 in the afternoon. That's about the time I arrived home.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say -- that's 16.00, 17.00 hours?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, about half past 4.00. 16.30 hours, approximately. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Today you've told us that you were responsible for the situation in the hotel. Can you tell us who was staying at the hotel at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time, there was the military police, a part of another army unit, the headquarters. I didn't have access to the military part, the part used by the army, so I cannot tell you what the names of the units were or of the commands, but it was army. It was the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Was the hotel used by other people who needed to stay there at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it your personnel that ran the hotel after the army settled in?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a headquarters; whose headquarters was it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I think General Blaskic's headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the military police. How many military policemen stayed at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't tell you exactly because I did not keep their records. I don't know how many there were. Every day I was presented with a count so that we could distribute meals, because they ate at the hotel, and some of them slept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that you didn't know, but can you tell me what these soldiers were doing in your hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. They kept guard, they had their desk at the door, they had some sentry posts outside, but I don't know what the sphere of their activity was. I was not a soldier. I was neither a member of the military police nor of the staff, so I cannot give you a precise answer. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know some of the people who were staying at your hotel? Did you have any previous acquaintance with them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: When did these soldiers start moving into your hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I think it was in the middle of 1993, but I can't tell you exactly. In the second half of 1992, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if they all arrived at the same time? You said the staff, you mentioned General Blaskic, you mentioned the military police; did they all arrive at the same time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: No. First, let us say -- I don't know how to describe them -- the municipal staff arrived, and 10 or 15 soldiers. Whether they were police or not, I don't know, because it was only after a certain time that the military police arrived. And in the autumn, General Blaskic arrived with his staff, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what rooms the military police occupied?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the military police had rooms behind the reception, and they were accommodated on the third floor of the accommodation facilities, and they used the restaurants for their meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You have already told us that you took care of their meals; do you know whether they slept in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I have just said, they were on the third floor. Whether it was just military police or whether there were other kinds of soldiers, I don't know, because that's what the agreement was. I didn't have any information about anything military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come to the hotel often before the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, every day, several times. Sometimes I would drop in two, three, four, five times, depending on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a desk; where was it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: It was by the reception, along the wall next to the reception desk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it at the very entrance to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, approximately at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And who was at that desk? Who was there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: The military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether, on the outside of the hotel, whether the military police guarded the hotel outside at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to ask you to recall and describe your arrival in the hotel on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 16th, I arrived at about a quarter past 6.00, or half past 6.00. I came under unusual circumstances. I was anxious, because there was gunfire all around. There were explosions, detonations. So it is very difficult to describe my arrival. I was afraid. I was in a panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say you arrived at a quarter past 6.00 or half past 6.00; where did you come from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I came from my old house in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How far is that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I think, if you take the shortcut, it's about one kilometre, or a kilometre and 200 metres. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So when did you wake up in the morning of the 16th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't an awakening. I was half asleep, because the circumstances were very unusual. My old house had been abandoned. So when I heard the detonations, of course at first I didn't know what was going on. I was afraid. I had to think about what to do, so a relative of mine and I left the old house and walked over the fields to the first Croatian village, Toljusici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, you said, "I was at my old house under unusual circumstances." I do not understand exactly what you were trying to say.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, then, I have to describe the previous day, the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you do it very briefly?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, when I came home from work, my wife, as usual, laid the table and put our dinner on the table. My youngest son was at the door, and he said to me that he could see a group of Muslim soldiers who were armed and were passing by my family house. I got up from the table, and I saw six or seven soldiers who were armed to the teeth, and they were carrying something on their backs. And later, I found out -- because I have just said that I am not a soldier -- but later I found out that these were hand-held rocket launchers, Zoljas or such, on their backs. They had automatic weapons. They set up a roadblock next to my house, some 20, 30 metres away, towards that part of the village which has a majority Croatian population. Then, for reasons of safety, I sent my wife and my youngest son to my brother's house, from where they went on some 700 to 800 metres to Vinko Miskovic's house, where I felt they would be safest.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, but whose army are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: The Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So when these detonations started, you sent your wife and children to a safer place; is that it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: No. On the 15th, at around 17.00 hours -- 17.30, I don't know, but it was around that time -- on the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So when you saw these soldiers and when you became concerned about their safety; is that it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, because such things had happened before. Roadblocks were set up in that part of the road, and I simply did not feel safe. I did not feel that my family was secure. I had experienced a lot of harassment, shooting, intimidation, around my house, and the most important thing to me was to protect my family. Believe it or not, I was not thinking of myself at the time, although today I think I was crazy. I stayed at my house in order, as I thought then, to protect my property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And then you decided to leave the old house and to go to Toljusici, and then you went toward the hotel; is that what you said? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I was around the house, my house, until about 10 or 11 p.m. -- that is, 22.00, 23.00 hours -- and the Muslim soldiers kept arriving. At one moment, because the main road runs some 10, 20 metres from my house, I felt there were 15, 20 soldiers there. And at the roadblock, I think there were as many as 30 or 40 of them, and they had either radio transmitters or Motorolas, walkie-talkies, I don't know. I just heard -- I heard the kind of sounds made when the police are chasing someone. I couldn't hear very well, because it was some 30 metres away from me. So for reasons of security, we withdrew to the old house, because the old house is about 150 metres distant from the house where we lived, on a hillside, so we thought that from there, we could watch and be safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So, excuse me, but you are talking about the evening of the 15th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we move through that time a bit faster and go on to the 16th?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, we spent the night there, and after the detonations at sunrise, I was half asleep because I was too frightened to really sleep, but I can't say that I did not drop off to sleep. But when we heard the detonations and when we realised that there were not just one or two but a lot of detonations, then we went to the village of Toljusici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And your relative was with you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you decide to go?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, we felt it was most important to reach safety, to get to the part of the village inhabited by Croats, and we arrived there. When we got to there, my relative stayed in Toljusici, and I went on to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: On that morning and on that road, were there any explosions, was there any gunfire? What did it look like then? Was it dangerous to go on foot, was it safe?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: It was still the dawn, and I was moving through a wood. I took a shortcut through a wood. It wasn't safe anywhere, but it was least safe in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say it was least safe in the town?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you decided to go to the town?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I went to the hotel, where I had to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why was it so important to you to expose yourself to the risk of going to work?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. As I have just said, I didn't know what was going on. Nothing like that had happened before. As you know in the former Yugoslavia, in the former system, in the former Yugoslav People's Army, we were taught that if there was any kind of emergency, the first thing we had to do was report to our workplace and everything else would follow from there. We would get instructions at our workplace. That was how it was in the former system, and this was something that was deeply imprinted in my mind, and I always tried to be very punctual about my job. I was fanatical, in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Your conscientiousness was sufficient reason for you to expose yourself to such a risk?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, when I think about it now, perhaps now I would behave differently. But at that time, I felt it was the only right thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that as a person who had responsibilities at your job and were responsible for your personnel, that you wanted to give the proper instructions to your personnel because, as you say, they were working and serving those who were staying at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the personnel was mixed. I mean they were of all the various ethnic origins.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why is it important? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you. It was important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you then please explain to me why it was important to you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time Croats and Muslims and Serbs worked to -- I and my personnel were given guarantees by the military police that nothing untoward would happen, and it is quite true that there were no problems. But there were the conditions of emergency, and I feared for the security -- for the safety of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but let us try to cut it shorter. So these were the principal reasons for you to go to the hotel that morning?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So around a quarter past 6.00 or half past 6.00, you were at the hotel, as you told us. Will you please describe to us how you arrived at the hotel? What entrance do you use to go into the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you that the town was the least safe place of all because there was fire all over the place. Bullets were whistling by, there were detonations, so the safest place was moving from one building to the other. And between the buildings, I managed to get to the hotel, and I entered through the main entrance to the receptionist.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you see there as you entered the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I saw the military policemen, that is, a couple of military policemen who were going out of the hotel, a couple of them going out. Some of them were in the lobby by the receptionist's, and that was about it. Panic reigned, fear, and I saw Mr. Santic, amongst others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll ask you about that later, but tell us something more about this. The hotel, was the hotel fired at, perhaps its front part, the glass? I mean it's mostly a glass-walled hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, on the front, yes, it is mostly glass panels, but also that part facing that part of the municipality controlled by the Muslim army, so that I didn't go there to that part, and nobody dared go. I wouldn't dare go there, and I had no need to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You said you met Vlado Santic there?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see that person here?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you see him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: To the left, next to the wall, I think the first one sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, may we then simply know that the witness recognised Vlado Santic here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you now tell us what you remember, if you remember anything, about the circumstances under which you saw Vlado Santic? Where was that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, as I entered the hotel, I already said I was frightened, I was afraid, and in the doorway or, rather, in the lobby between the reception desk and the restaurant, in the lobby there, I met -- I saw Vlado, not Vlado only, but I talked to Vlado because he was the one I knew best of them. So I asked him, "Vlado, what is this? What's going on?" He drew -- I did not think it was a particularly nice way to respond, but he only -- at least I thought it like that, but he simply waved his hand and said, "Well, don't you see? What are you asking me about that," and that was the end of this conversation. I went on through the restaurant to the kitchen to see if there were any of the personnel there, per chance. But as none of them were there, I just turned and left the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you spent a very short time in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you, just as long as it was necessary for me to go in. I had this contact with Vlado, perhaps it would have been better if I hadn't, and I went to the kitchen, checked if there were any of the personnel there. And as there was nobody there, I left the hotel, because at that time I had nothing to do there. There was nothing for me to do there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to this. You said Vlado Santic didn't treat you particularly nice at that time, did he?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. My feeling was that he was also frightened, that he was afraid, upset or something. He looked upset to me. I don't think there was any need for him to -- or at least I expected that he would perhaps devote some time to me, share perhaps a few more words with me or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But perhaps the circumstances would not permit him to conduct a conversation with you or something?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, now, of course, I realise that the circumstances would not allow us to have a chat, but at that time I simply did not -- it did not penetrate, because I asked -- I was at a loss. I didn't know what was happening, what was going on, and I wanted somebody to tell me what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps your wish to find out what was going on might have been also another reason for you to go to the hotel, because you believed you would find there people from whom you could learn something more?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, quite possible. That is quite possible that that was one of the reasons for which I went there. But to be quite honest, I'm telling you my principal -- the principal motive for me was to get to my work, and then all the rest of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right, yes, thank you. You've told us that already. But will you tell us if you knew Vlado before that day that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that it was from childhood days, but for a very long time, since elementary school, since grade school, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you went to the same school?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: No, I mean we could have been enrolled in the same school, but we are not peers, we are not of the same generation. But Vitez is a small town, so naturally everybody knows everybody, so I knew Vlado and I know his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, however cursory that meeting with Vlado that morning and, as you said, not particularly friendly, could you perhaps try to remember, what was Vlado wearing then?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I believe -- well, to my mind, he was dressed as usual, wearing a camouflage uniform. True, as far as I remember, he did not have a cap on his head at the time, which if I were a soldier, if I were a military, that would be something that I couldn't explain, I mean something --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But you say that you are not a military, and therefore it is easy to explain that fact, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Franjic, you say "as usual". You mean his appearance was the same as when you saw him in the hotel on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you distinguish between that military appearance and the appearance in combat? I mean you've seen films, so could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I could make a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Did Vlado Santic have any weapons on him that morning, any arms?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I believe he had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could we say that it was a pistol as was usually kept by the military police and held by the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: After that encounter, when you started towards the restaurant and then left the hotel quickly, did you then still see Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Vlado stayed behind there in the lobby. He was issuing some instructions or some guidelines. I don't know. He was waving his hands about. I said I needed -- I left the facility immediately because I was truly afraid. I cannot really claim, but he -- yes, he stayed behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did anyone else at that time, as you were coming out of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I don't think there was another military policeman there who might have been moving, going to those guard posts, but I was really very fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you allow the possibility for the guards, that they may have been going to those guard posts which you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know really. I mean military police were milling about. I don't really know who was going out or coming in. Somebody might have gone to the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But did you come to the hotel again that day?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So after what you told us, that you saw Vlado Santic, did you see him again after the 16th? If "Yes", when was that after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I cannot really claim that I saw him, because I did not have much opportunity of going down to Vitez. Every seven or ten days or so would I go down for a couple of hours. We would go down there to wash, perhaps get a shave, so that I had no opportunity or time to go to the hotel. That is just to drop in and see my family, nothing else. So I know I saw him sometime midway through the war. I think it was autumn. I think it was sometime midway through the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You say "autumn". Which year was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Why do you remember that meeting with Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I feel rather embarrassed talking about this because these times are past, but if you want me to tell you about that, that was another rather awkward meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if it won't take you long to tell us.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Oh, come, it won't. I said that I would go home every seven or ten days, but I was very ill then, I was running a high fever, so I went to see a doctor, and I came home and went to bed. The military police came to my door and asked me to tell them where the truck of the Kruscica company was or, rather, where its keys were, because they wanted to requisition it for the military police. As I told you, I was born in Kruscica, I'm a child of Kruscica. That company had paid for my education. I have never known another company. I worked in Kruscica all my life, all my working life. So I refused to give them the keys and I resisted to tell them where the truck was. But they knew where that truck was, and when I told them, "No," they said, "Why do we ask you for it? Let's go and take that vehicle by ourselves." And even though I was feverish, I went to that place. I got up and went to that place, and there was a rather undesirable situation. That is, it almost came to fisticuffs with the military policemen, because I did not want to give them that vehicle. Then they went to Vlado, and Vlado either issued an order or perhaps a letter, but a handwritten letter without seal or stamp or anything, that that vehicle was being requisitioned for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: And you were angry with Vlado Santic?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, the next day a quarrel broke out between Vlado Santic and me, and true, after that brief altercation, after that brief argument, the keys of the car were returned to me and the vehicle was taken back to that same site next to the driver's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But are you aware that under wartime conditions, vehicles may be requisitioned for the army? Naturally, a proper document needs to be issued for that and these vehicles are then returned, of course, if they survive.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course, I'm aware of that now. But at that time, believe me, nobody could put it over to me, and I was rather stubborn, pig-headed, when it came to the company's property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So perhaps Vlado Santic and the others had to do it because that was a war necessity.

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, today when I think about it, of course, yes. But at that time, I simply did not think that was all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm trying to say is that it was not a confiscation, even if you were not given an official paper?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you now, when I think about it, of course it was not a confiscation or anything like that or a robbery, but at that time it wasn't only that. I resisted when they wanted to requisition my rooms. I thought a mass confiscation for the military needs. I said, "Well, the war is not going to last for very long, and one will have to live after that again."

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So you just behaved as an owner who wanted to keep it all safe?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, you can put it that way, yes, and I believed I was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Franjic. I have two more questions, Mr. President. The first one:

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed today that Vlado Santic, whom you know, is in the courtroom today. Do you know, because you were born in Vitez or, rather, in those environs, do you know any other individual of that same first and last name?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do these individuals live in or around Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us if those individuals lived there at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: My second question: You know where the village of Ahmici is?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So today, if we go from Vitez to Ahmici on foot, taking the main road, how long do we need?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I've never walked to Ahmici by the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: But at that time, could one use the main road to walk from Vitez to Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think a normal man would do that or would use that particular road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that road pass through or by villages held by Muslims at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does, by localities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: "By localities." Could you mention the names of some of them?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Well, one of the nearest ones is the Sivrino Selo which comes before, which is between Vitez and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if one could go through Sivrino Selo without incurring a risk and then going on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Through Sivrino Selo, no way, and not even that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But Sivrino Selo is off the road?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's the first houses from which they acted, where those Muslim forces were, so perhaps 50 metres from the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So the road was within the range and they could hit anyone moving on that road?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, in other words, that this was not a safe way to Ahmici, that one had to take some other route?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: So was there some roundabout route which could serve as an alternative and which had been built before, I mean that could be used on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA FRANJIC
utterances.text: No, not really. There was partly a road to the village of Rijeka, to a stream or a brook or a creek. I don't know what to call it. I think it's called the Vranjska River, or something like that; I don't know. And from there on you would have to cut across meadows. That is, as that particular vehicle moved, they built the road. Perhaps -- I don't really know whether it was a wheat field or a meadow, but there has never been path, a road, or anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Thank you, Mr. Franjic. I have no more questions for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. Mr. Blaxill or Mr. Terrier, I assume you would need more than seven minutes for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I will do my best to be quick, but seven minutes would be unrealistic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. So let us adjourn now, and we will see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: I'm obliged to you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAXILL
utterances.text: 12.53 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 9th day of July, 1999, at 9.00 a.m.
